analysis.one_liner: Pays states to replace cash bail with risk-based pretrial release decisions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a small federal grant program, about $15 million a year, to help states and Indian tribes replace money bail with a system where judges decide pretrial release based on each person's risk of skipping court or committing a new crime. Grant recipients would have to move toward releasing most defendants quickly, giving every defendant a lawyer at the first hearing, and using the least restrictive supervision necessary. It would also fund a national program to collect data on how courts process defendants before trial.
analysis.who_benefits: People arrested but not yet convicted who cannot afford to pay bail, a group that is disproportionately Black and Hispanic and overwhelmingly poor. The bill's own findings note that about 9 in 10 detained defendants had bail set but could not pay it, and that even a few days in jail can cost someone their job, housing, or child custody. Taxpayers also benefit, since jailing people awaiting trial costs roughly $14 billion a year nationally. Communities may be safer, because the findings cite research that high-risk defendants with money can buy their way out while low-risk defendants who are jailed briefly become more likely to reoffend.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Poor defendants jailed for lack of bail money

how_it_helps.text: Replaces secured money bail with individualized, research-validated risk assessments and a presumption of release in most cases, with preventive detention allowed only after a hearing with counsel and clear and convincing evidence [S3].
Requires grant recipients to provide a lawyer to 100 percent of defendants at their first court appearance and to set release conditions that do not impose additional charges on the defendant [S3].

Sets performance benchmarks, including 95 percent court-appearance rates, release rates of at least 85 percent, and detention hearings within 3 to 7 days of arrest, with annual reporting broken down by race, sex, age, and disability [S3].
Funds a National Pretrial Reporting Program to collect data on how state and local courts process defendants before trial [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal taxpayer, through appropriations of $15 million in fiscal year 2018, and to a lesser extent the commercial bail bond industry, which loses the business of jurisdictions that switch to nonfinancial release. Some defense and civil-liberties advocates have also worried generally that risk-assessment tools could bake in existing racial bias, and the bill tries to address that by requiring locally validated tools and annual bias reporting.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; the bail bond industry

drawbacks.text: The grant program is small, about $15 million against a $14 billion annual national cost of jailing pretrial defendants, and grants are permissive, so states could decline to make the deeper system changes the bill envisions [S3].

The bill relies on risk-assessment tools, which critics across the political spectrum have warned can inherit bias from arrest and conviction data; the bill requires local validation and anti-disparity reporting but does not guarantee the tools will be fair [S3].
It is an incentive program, not a mandate, so it cannot itself free anyone from jail; its effect depends entirely on states choosing to apply and then to reform their own systems [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea addresses a well-documented harm: jailing unconvicted people because they cannot pay, with evidence in the bill's findings of lost jobs, higher reoffending, and racial disparities in bail amounts. The main weaknesses are scale and design: the funding is tiny relative to the problem, participation is voluntary, and risk-assessment tools carry real fairness risks the bill mitigates with validation and reporting requirements but does not eliminate. On balance the benefits to poor defendants, taxpayers, and possibly public safety outweigh the modest costs, though the bill is a nudge rather than a fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in July 2017, and the committee never acted on it; the bill died there when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Kamala Harris introduced the bill with Sen. Rand Paul as the sole cosponsor, making it a bipartisan introduction [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and there were no further actions before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The commercial bail bond industry keeps its market intact, since no jurisdiction faced federal incentives to move away from cash bail. Poor defendants in states without independent reform gains gained nothing; taxpayers continued paying roughly $14 billion a year to jail people awaiting trial, per the bill's own findings [S3].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The bail bond industry; jailed defendants gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a bipartisan introduction with one Democrat and one Republican, but with no votes ever taken the record shows no partisan split on the merits.

industries.note: Cash bail is the business model of commercial bail: defendants or their families pay bondsmen a nonrefundable fee, typically around 10 percent, to secure release. Every jurisdiction that replaces cash bail with nonfinancial release eliminates that revenue stream, so the industry's interest runs directly against poor defendants' interest in release without payment.

industries.industry: Pretrial risk-assessment software and supervision providers
industries.note: Replacing cash bail with risk-based decision making creates demand for validated assessment tools, electronic reminders, and pretrial supervision services. That could benefit defendants if done well, but it also substitutes a new gatekeeping industry for the old one, which is why the bill requires local validation, prohibits charging defendants for supervision, and mandates annual bias reporting [S3].
